newsitem.title: THAILAND: Non-performing Thai bank loans surprise analysts.
newsitem.headline: Non-performing Thai bank loans surprise analysts.

text.p: The Bank of Thailand on Friday reported bigger than expected non-performing loans in the banking sector, adding to market concerns about short-term prospects of financial institutions.
The central bank said non-performing loans of 14 Thai commercial banks averaged 7.73 percent of their total outstanding credits at end-June, up from 6.92 percent at end-1995.

Thirachai Phuvanardnaranubal, director of the central bank's supervision and development of financial institutions, said he expected banks to post improved performance next year as the Thai economic slowdown showed signs of bottoming out.
The official said the end-June figure was lower than those posted by Malaysian and Indonesian banks.
The central bank figure surprised some analysts who said it would likely be reflected on weaker bank earnings next year and may induce further sales of bank shares early next week.

Piti Sithi-Amnuai, executive vice chairman of Bangkok Bank Plc, said: "Thai banks have made adequate provisions although some are only at bare minimums...we have gulped down a lot that was not so good this year and at least we can sleep at night."
The banker was surprised the central bank announced the previously confidential figure. He said it would now be to up to each Thai bank to disclose its exposure.

The central bank announcement came amid market concerns this week about the quality of property loans extended by banks. The jitters triggered an active sell-off of bank stocks that helped pull the overall market to a 51-month low on Friday.
Thailand's slowing economic growth, prolonged property sector slump, and sluggish exports have contributed to sustained stock market setbacks in recent months.

"The figure is only up to mid-year and I expect it has worsened since, although some portion of it may be backed by collateral...this will send analysts back to revise their forecasts," said analyst Andrew Maule of Nithipat Capital.
